findings.explanation: ATS is turned off app-wide, permitting plaintext HTTP and weak TLS to any host. Traffic can be intercepted/modified on hostile networks.
findings.remediation: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads. Serve all traffic over HTTPS with TLS 1.2+, and scope any unavoidable exception to a specific domain via NSExceptionDomains.
findings.title: App Transport Security globally disabled (NSAllowsArbitraryLoads)
findings.why: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads removes the HTTPS floor for every domain, so any request the app makes over http:// or weak TLS can be read and altered on the path. Connections that use HTTPS stay encrypted, and the scan cannot say what, if anything, the app sends in cleartext, so confidentiality and integrity are scored low (convention point 2); the breadth - every domain rather than listed exceptions - does not change what is exposed per request.

findings.explanation: WKWebView is the iOS embedded browser.
findings.title: WKWebView in use
findings.why: The app embeds a WebView.

findings.explanation: The app registers custom URL scheme(s) via CFBundleURLSchemes. Any app or web page can invoke these; if application(_:open:options:) acts on unvalidated parameters, this is an entry point for unauthorized actions. Custom schemes are also unverified (unlike Universal Links). Review the handler for input validation.
findings.remediation: Validate and sanitize every parameter in application(_:open:options:); never trigger sensitive actions from a URL without authentication. Prefer Universal Links (verified) over custom schemes.
findings.title: Registers 7 custom URL schemes (inbound deep-link surface)
findings.why: The app registers custom URL schemes. MASWE-0029 makes them a weakness when a sensitive flow relies on them or the handler does not validate input, which MASTG-TEST-0370 and -0371 read from the handler code.

findings.explanation: The bundle contains http:// URLs for 2 host(s): tizen.org, www.apache.org. A hard-coded cleartext URL is a place the app may talk to a server without TLS. Whether it does depends on how the URL is used and on the ATS configuration, which blocks cleartext loads through URLSession unless an exception allows them.
findings.remediation: Switch each URL to https://, and remove any ATS exception that only exists to keep a cleartext endpoint working.
findings.title: Hard-coded cleartext http:// URLs (2 hosts)
findings.why: MASTG notes that an http:// URL in the bundle does not show it is used for communication; the scan records the candidates.

findings.explanation: References NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey / isExcludedFromBackup. The key does not guarantee exclusion, and sensitive files still need to be encrypted, so its presence is a reference, not a mitigation.
findings.title: Backup-exclusion API in use (NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey)
findings.why: Records that the app marks files as excluded from backup.

findings.explanation: A binary imports NSFileProtectionNone, the class that leaves a file readable while the device is locked. The import shows the option is referenced, often by a library that maps every protection class; whether it is applied to sensitive data needs the manual review the linked MASTG test describes.
findings.title: References NSFileProtectionNone
findings.why: The import shows the protection class is referenced, not that sensitive data is stored under it.

findings.explanation: A binary imports kSecAttrAccessibleAlways or its ThisDeviceOnly variant, the deprecated accessibility classes that keep a Keychain item readable while the device is locked. Keychain wrapper libraries import them to map every class, so whether an item is stored this way needs the manual review the linked MASTG test describes.
findings.title: References kSecAttrAccessibleAlways
findings.why: The import shows the accessibility class is referenced, not that an item is stored under it.

findings.explanation: Imports rand() / srand() / random() / drand48(), predictable PRNGs unsuitable for tokens, keys, IVs or nonces. Use SecRandomCopyBytes or arc4random_buf. `arc4random() % n` also introduces modulo bias; prefer arc4random_uniform(n).
findings.title: Non-cryptographic random number generator
findings.why: A non-cryptographic generator is linked. MASTG-TEST-0311 fails only when its output is used for keys, tokens or other security values, which is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Imports CC_MD5 / CC_SHA1 (CommonCrypto) or CryptoKit's Insecure.MD5 / Insecure.SHA1. Both are collision-broken and unsuitable for signatures, integrity checks or password hashing, but are also widely used for non-security purposes (cache keys, ETags, file checksums), so the finding is a pointer for review.
findings.title: Weak hash primitive (MD5 / SHA-1)
findings.why: MD5 or SHA-1 is linked. MASTG-TEST-0211 fails only when the hash protects sensitive data; checksums and cache keys pass. That use is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: application-groups entitlement allows multiple apps from the same publisher to share UserDefaults/files (often used to share IDFA / VPN-detected flag between sibling apps).
findings.title: App Groups entitlement (cross-app data sharing)
findings.why: Shared container between the vendor's own apps.

findings.explanation: aps-environment entitlement, push notifications.
findings.title: APS push environment
findings.why: Push environment the build targets.

findings.explanation: The binary imports dlopen/dlsym, so it can resolve and call code chosen at runtime rather than at link time. That is how optional frameworks, plugin architectures and A/B-tested SDKs are loaded, and it is entirely normal, so this ships as INFO inventory rather than a weakness. It matters only as context: an app that also carries obfuscation (SURV-04) or a data broker (TRK-02) can assemble behaviour a static scan cannot see, and dynamic code loading is the mechanism that makes that possible. Note the limit of the signal: an import proves the symbol is linked, not that it is ever called, and iOS forbids loading code that is not already in the signed bundle. (MASWE-0049)
findings.title: Dynamic loader in use (dlopen / dlsym)
findings.why: dlopen/dlsym are present in the binary.

findings.explanation: keychain-access-groups, shares keychain entries across same-publisher apps.
findings.title: Keychain access group (cross-app credential share)
findings.why: Credential sharing between the vendor's own apps.

findings.explanation: com.apple.developer.associated-domains, handles universal links / web credentials.
findings.title: Associated domains / universal links
findings.why: Associated domains the app claims.

findings.explanation: Imports SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags, which binds a Keychain item or key to user presence, biometrics or the device passcode. A positive signal; which flags are passed cannot be read from the symbol table.
findings.title: Keychain access control in use (SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags)
findings.why: A positive signal: Keychain items are access-control bound.

findings.explanation: Uses the Keychain Services API (SecItemAdd / SecItemCopyMatching / SecItemUpdate). Informational, pair with SECH-02.keychain_accessible_always to judge whether items are protected with an appropriate accessibility / access-control class.
findings.title: Keychain API in use (SecItem)
findings.why: A positive signal: the app uses the Keychain.

findings.explanation: Third-party code from AppsFlyer (IL) is embedded via 1 SDK(s): AppsFlyer. Each embedded SDK is a supply-chain dependency that can collect data and update its own behaviour.
findings.remediation: Inventory embedded SDKs and their data collection; remove unused SDKs and pin/verify their distribution to reduce supply-chain exposure.
findings.title: Embedded SDK provenance: AppsFlyer
findings.why: An inventory of who owns the embedded SDKs. Ownership is not a weakness; data-broker and AI recipients carry their own findings under TRK-02 and TRK-05.

findings.explanation: Imports the C function getifaddrs() which lists every network interface. NOTE: getifaddrs is also the standard primitive for plain reachability and local-IP discovery and is linked by many networking SDKs, so the import alone is a weak VPN signal that fires on most apps. MASTG / privacy-guide VPN detection keys on NEVPNManager or an explicit tunnel-interface name (utun/ppp/ipsec), kept here as an informational marker only.
findings.title: Imports getifaddrs() for network interface enumeration
findings.why: Reading network interfaces and proxy settings on the device meets none of the WP248 criteria by itself.

findings.explanation: Calls CFNetworkCopySystemProxySettings or reads HTTP proxy keys, often used to detect that the user has interception/SOCKS/HTTP proxy enabled.
findings.title: Reads system proxy settings

findings.explanation: Calls _dyld_image_count / _dyld_get_image_name, can be used to detect injected dylibs (tweaks, Frida gadget). findings.explanation: The bundle references 1 endpoint(s) whose owner is based in IL, owners: AppsFlyer. The country is the owning organisation's home jurisdiction from the tracker database, not where a server is hosted, and a referenced endpoint is not observed traffic. If the app sends personal data there, it is a third-country transfer: whether that is lawful depends on the safeguards, purpose and paperwork behind it, none of which is visible in a binary. IL holds an EU adequacy decision, so a transfer there needs no additional Chapter V safeguard. Tracker-class endpoints are among the destinations.

findings.explanation: The bundle references 2 endpoint(s) whose owner is based in US, owners: Apple, Arkose Labs. The country is the owning organisation's home jurisdiction from the tracker database, not where a server is hosted, and a referenced endpoint is not observed traffic. findings.explanation: The main Mach-O is encrypted by the App Store. Static string scanning of its TEXT segment won't work without a decrypted dump (e.g., via frida-ios-dump or bagbak on a jailbroken device). Embedded frameworks and dylibs are USUALLY ENCRYPTED TOO (measured 91% across the reference corpus; in half of apps every Mach-O is encrypted), so TEXT-segment string recall is limited bundle-wide, not just for the main binary. What still survives encryption is __LINKEDIT: symbols, imported/defined symbol names, ObjC selectors and linked dylibs, which is why symbol-based detection carries this scan rather than string matching.
findings.remediation: For full TEXT-segment coverage, supply a decrypted .ipa produced by frida-ios-dump or bagbak from a jailbroken device. Resource files, plists, entitlements, symbols, selectors and linked dylibs are still scanned in the meantime.

findings.explanation: Apple requires apps that use this category of API to declare it in PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy with a justified reason. Indicator(s) for Disk space (systemFreeSize / systemSize / volumeAvailableCapacity*Key / volumeTotalCapacityKey / statfs / fstatfs / statvfs / fstatvfs) appear in 1 framework(s), but the Privacy Manifest does not declare `NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryDiskSpace`. This is an App-Store-policy compliance gap.
